subject: Agriculture
title: Sorghum and Millet
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Sorghum and Millet.

hook.text: Sorghum and millet feed 500 million people in Africa and Asia—but get almost no research funding.

buildup.text: These grains thrive in hot, dry conditions where wheat and rice fail. They're the crops of the poorest regions.

discovery.text: Sorghum is C4 and extremely water-efficient. Pearl millet can grow with just 250mm of annual rainfall.

twist.text: As climate change makes droughts more common, sorghum and millet may become more important, not less.

climax.text: India declared 2023 the UN Year of Millets, pushing these 'orphan crops' into the global spotlight.

punchline.text: The crops we ignored may be the ones we'll need most.

quiz.question: Why might sorghum and millet become more important under climate change?
options: They thrive in hot, dry conditions where wheat and rice fail

details.summary: Sorghum and millet are drought-tolerant cereal grains vital to food security in Africa and Asia. This topic covers their agronomy, nutritional value, traditional uses, and why these 'climate-smart' grains are attracting renewed global interest.
details.whyItMatters: As water scarcity worsens, sorghum and millet offer proven resilience in arid conditions where corn and rice fail. They may become critical staples as climates become hotter and drier.
takeaways: Sorghum and millets feed over 500 million people in semi-arid regions
These grains require 40–50% less water than maize to produce a harvest
The UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets to boost awareness

faq.question: Why are sorghum and millet considered climate-smart crops?
faq.answer: Both crops have evolved deep root systems, waxy leaves that reduce water loss, and the ability to go dormant during drought then resume growth when rains return. They produce yields in conditions too harsh for corn, wheat, or rice.

faq.question: What are the nutritional benefits of millet?
faq.answer: Millets are rich in fiber, iron, calcium, and B vitamins. They are naturally gluten-free, have a lower glycemic index than rice, and provide balanced protein with essential amino acids, making them highly nutritious staple grains.
